artifacts.title: UCUM -- Unified Code for Units of Measure, essence file, version 2.2
artifacts.licence: UCUM is published under its own licence by the Regenstrief Institute and the UCUM Organization; freely usable with attribution.
satisfies: FR-0.1 (partial) -- independent corroboration of unit-equivalence labels
why_this_matters: FR-0.1 wants the equivalence suite dual-labelled by someone who did not write the
comparator, and no second person is available. UCUM is maintained by a standards committee
with no connection to this project and publishes EXACT conversion values, so for the subset
of the suite that turns on a question of fact -- is 0.5 in the same length as 12.7 mm -- it
can adjudicate independently. Read by errata_bench.ucum, which deliberately does NOT use
Pint: errata_valuesem resolves through Pint, so a Pint-based corroborator would be asking
one library the same question twice and reporting the echo as validation.

artifacts.title: NBS Handbook H28 (1957) Part I -- Screw-Thread Standards for Federal Services
artifacts.licence: United States Government publication (National Bureau of Standards, Dept of Commerce). PUBLIC DOMAIN.
satisfies: FR-0.1 (partial) -- independent corroboration of Unified inch thread labels
why_this_matters: ASME B1.1 is the current Unified-thread standard and is paywalled, which is why the threads
family had no external source beyond the metric cases ISO 261 covers.
NBS Handbook H28 is a US Government publication in the PUBLIC DOMAIN, covers the same
UNC/UNF/UNEF series, and is the document ASME B1.1 descends from. That is the general
trick and it is worth remembering: where a current standard is paywalled, the federal or
national standard covering the same subject frequently is not.
Adding it took the threads family from 38 externally-judged cases to 58, and total
corroboration coverage from 14.6% to 17.8%.

verified_contents.table_III_3_p25: Coarse thread series UNC and NC -- size, threads per inch, thread symbol
verified_contents.table_III_4_pp25_26: Fine thread series UNF and NF
verified_contents.table_III_5_p26: Extra-fine thread series UNEF and NEF

read_how: VISUALLY, from rendered page images -- not from the OCR text layer. The OCR on this 1957
scan renders 40 as '4b' and 56 as '6', which is exactly the kind of plausible-wrong number
that ground rule 1 exists to keep out. Same method used for ISO 261 Table 2.
deliberate_omissions: #4 UNC and #6 UNF are smudged past legibility in this scan and are NOT recorded. Their
values are well known, and 'well known' is precisely how an unread number gets written down
as though it had been read. The adjudicator declines both rather than asserting them.
artifacts.incidental_confirmation: HANDOFF section 7 records an earlier session 'briefly wrote UNF's 12 TPI values into the UNEF table, where the correct value is 18'. Both tables confirm it and show how it happened: from 1 inch upward UNF runs 12 and UNEF runs 18, in adjacent columns of adjacent pages.

artifacts.title: UNSPSC codeset -- United Nations Standard Products and Services Code, four levels, published as open data by the State of Oklahoma (OMES)
artifacts.licence: UNSPSC(R) is published by GS1 US. This file is a public-sector republication by the Oklahoma Office of Management and Enterprise Services on data.ok.gov; the portal records no licence id. NOT REDISTRIBUTED -- this repository stores the URL and content hash only (FR-9.5), and the bridge cites individual codes as evidence in the way a standard's clause is cited.
satisfies: FR-9.7 -- the ETIM<->UNSPSC attribute bridge needs a UNSPSC side that was actually opened
provenance_caveat: THIS IS A PUBLIC-SECTOR REPUBLICATION, NOT unspsc.org. The official codeset download is
behind a registration form; a state procurement portal publishes the same four-level code
list as open data, which is a source that can be fetched, hashed and re-fetched by a third
party reproducing our scores -- the FR-9.5 property that matters here.
The portal's metadata records metadata_modified 2019-10-31, so this is a 2019-vintage
snapshot of a codeset that is revised roughly annually. That is stated rather than elided:
the bridge pins the codes it uses by both code AND title, and errata_ecosystem.bridge
refuses to load a mapping whose title no longer matches the codeset it is validated
against, so a newer UNSPSC release produces a failure rather than a silent drift.
Under ground rule 1 this is a source actually opened, and its status is stated.

verified_contents.note: Read on 2026-08-20. Four levels, eight-digit codes, NO attribute layer of any kind -- which is the hole FR-9.7 exists to fill, confirmed by inspection rather than from the PRD's say-so.
